column2: Blindness, dullness and sharpness are properties of the eye, according to its good or bad condition; so too deafness, dumbness and the like are properties of the ear and the other organs — not of the knower, the Self.
Inhaling, exhaling, yawning, sneezing, secretion, departure and the like are the functions of the breath, say those who know; hunger and thirst are properties of the breath.
The inner organ abides in these — the eye and the rest, and in the body — through the identification "I", with the light of reflected consciousness.
That is to be known as ego, the agent and enjoyer with self-conceit; by its association with the qualities beginning with sattva, it goes through the three states.
When objects are favourable it is happy, when adverse it is unhappy; pleasure and pain are its properties, not of the Self, whose nature is ever bliss.
An object is dear only for the sake of the Self; it is not dear in itself. Since the Self is by itself dearest to all, therefore the Self is ever bliss and has no pain at any time.
The bliss of the Self is experienced in deep sleep when there is no object; in the waking state scripture, direct perception, tradition and inference (confirm it).

The supreme power of the Lord, called the Unmanifest, beginningless ignorance, made of the three qualities, is Maya — to be inferred by the wise from its effects — by which this whole world is brought forth.
It is neither existent nor non-existent nor both; neither different nor non-different nor both; neither with parts nor without parts nor both — wonderful, of an indescribable nature.
It is destroyed by the knowledge of pure, non-dual Brahman, as the snake-delusion by discrimination of the rope. Its qualities, famous as rajas, tamas and sattva, are known by their own effects.

The projecting power belongs to rajas, of the nature of activity; from it the ancient stream of activity has flowed out. From it always arise passion and the like, and the pains and other modifications of the mind.
Desire, anger, greed, hypocrisy, envy, egoism, jealousy and the like are terrible; these are the properties of rajas, from which arises a person's activity; therefore rajas is the cause of bondage.

The power called veiling belongs to the quality of tamas, by which a thing appears otherwise than it is; this is the origin of a person's worldly existence, and the cause of the further spread of the projecting power.

Even a wise, learned and clever man, whose vision of the very subtle Self is licked by tamas, does not clearly understand though taught in many ways; he thinks what is imagined through delusion to be real and clings to its qualities. Alas, mighty is the great veiling power of the dreadful tamas!
Non-conception, wrong conception, doubt and misapprehension are its (effects); the projecting power, joined with them, certainly does not let go and ceaselessly wears one out.
Ignorance, laziness, dullness, sleep, negligence, stupidity and the like are the properties of tamas; driven by them one knows nothing and remains like a sleeper or a post.
Sattva is pure like water, yet when mixed with the two others it is fit to be a means of worldly movement; in it the reflection of the Self, shining, illumines the whole inert world like the sun.
The properties of mixed sattva are humility and the like, the restraints and observances, faith, devotion, longing for liberation, divine wealth, and turning away from the unreal.

The qualities of pure sattva are serenity, experience of one's own Self, supreme peace, contentment, great joy, and steadfastness in the Supreme Self, by which one attains the taste of ever-lasting bliss.
This Unmanifest, described as of three qualities, is called the causal body of the Self. Deep sleep is its distinct state, in which all activities of the senses and the intellect have dissolved.
The cessation of all kinds of knowledge, the intellect's abiding only in seed form — that is deep sleep, whose experience is known in the world by the statement "I knew nothing."

Body, senses, breath, mind, ego and the rest, all modifications, objects, pleasure and the like, the elements beginning with space and the whole universe, up to the Unmanifest — all this is the not-Self.
Maya and all the effects of Maya, from the Great Principle down to the body — know this not-Self to be unreal, like a mirage in the desert.
Now I shall tell you the nature of the Supreme Self, knowing which a man is freed from bondage and attains isolation.
There is someone, self-existent and eternal, who is the ground of the sense of "I," the witness of the three states, and distinct from the five sheaths.
He who knows everything in the states of waking, dream and deep sleep — the presence and the absence of the intellect and its activities — this is the "I."
He who sees everything by himself, whom no one sees; who makes the intellect and the rest aware, but is not made aware by them.
By whom this universe is pervaded, but whom nothing pervades; whose light all this reflects, and who, shining, is followed by all that shines.
By whose mere presence the body, senses, mind and intellect go about their own objects as if impelled.
By whom, whose nature is eternal knowledge, are known, like a pot, the objects, pleasure and the like, from ego down to the body.
This inner Self, the ancient Person, of continuous, unbroken bliss, ever of one form, mere awareness — by him speech and the breaths, being sent, move.
Here, in the cave of the intellect, whose nature is sattva, in the undifferentiated space, he shines radiant; like the sun, high in the sky, he illumines this universe by his own light.
The knower of the modifications of mind and ego and of the actions performed by body, senses and breath, he follows them like fire in iron, but does not act and does not change at all.
He is not born, does not die, does not grow, does not decay, does not change; he is eternal. Even when this body dissolves, he does not dissolve, like the space in a pot.

Different from Nature and its modifications, of the nature of pure awareness, revealing all this, existent and non-existent, without distinction, the Supreme Self shines in the states of waking and the rest, directly as "I, I," in the form of the witness of the intellect.

With a controlled mind, know directly this Self in your own self as "this is I," through the clearness of the intellect. Cross the shoreless ocean of worldly existence, with its waves of birth and death, become fulfilled, abiding as Brahman.

The idea "I" in the not-Self is the bondage of this person, arisen from ignorance, the cause of falling into the pains of birth and death, by which he cherishes, anoints and guards this unreal body as if it were the Self, entangled by objects like a silkworm by its threads.

Through tamas, in the deluded, arises the notion of the (Self) in what is not that, as through lack of discrimination the idea of a rope flashes upon a snake; then a host of evils falls upon the man — listen, friend: this taking of the unreal (for the real) is bondage.
This veiling power, made of tamas, covers the Self, shining with the power of undivided, eternal, non-dual knowledge and of infinite glory, like Rahu covering the sun's disc.

When the Self, of most stainless radiance, is hidden, a man through delusion thinks the body, the not-Self, to be "I"; then the great power of rajas called projection torments him with the bonds of desire, anger and the like.

Having lost the knowledge of the Self, seized by the crocodile of great delusion, this man of poor understanding, himself acting out the various states of the intellect by identification with its qualities, dives and rises in the shoreless ocean of worldly existence, filled with the poison of objects, and wanders on a bad path.
As a bank of clouds produced by the sun's rays covers the sun and spreads, so the ego arising from the Self covers the truth of the Self and spreads.

As on a dark day, when the sun is swallowed by dense clouds, the fierce cold storm-wind torments them, so, when the Self is covered by unbroken darkness, the sharp power of projection wears out the deluded mind with many sorrows.
It is through these two powers that bondage has come upon man, by which, deluded, he thinks the body to be the Self and wanders.

Tamas is the seed of the tree of worldly existence; the idea of the body as the Self is the sprout; attachment the tender leaves; action the water; the body the trunk; the breaths the branches; the collection of senses the twigs; objects the flowers; suffering the fruit, of many kinds, born of various actions; and the individual soul, the enjoyer, is the bird in it.
This bondage to the not-Self, rooted in ignorance, is called natural, beginningless and endless; it produces for the soul a flood of the sufferings of birth, death, disease, old age and so on.
It cannot be cut by missiles or weapons, by wind or fire, or by crores of works; only by the great sword of discriminating knowledge, sharp and polished, by the grace of the Creator.

For one whose mind holds only to the authority of scripture, there is steadfastness in his own duty, and by that alone comes the purification of the self; for one of pure intellect, knowledge of the Supreme Self, and by that alone the uprooting of worldly existence.
The Self, covered by the five sheaths beginning with the food-made, does not shine — as water in a tank does not, covered by a layer of moss produced by its own power.
When that moss is removed, the pure water is properly seen, which removes the heat of thirst and at once gives supreme happiness to a person.
When the five sheaths are set aside, this (Self) shines — pure, of one taste of eternal bliss, the inmost, the supreme, self-luminous.
Discrimination between the Self and the not-Self is to be practised by the wise for release from bondage; by it alone one becomes blissful, having known one's own being-consciousness-bliss.

He who, separating the Self from the visible world, as a reed's inner stalk from its sheath — the inmost Self, unattached, actionless — and dissolving everything in it, stays as that Self, is liberated.
This body, the dwelling of food, the sheath made of food, lives by food and perishes without it; being a heap of skin, flesh, blood, bone and dung, it cannot possibly be the ever-pure Self.

It did not exist before birth and does not after death; it exists only from the moment of birth, momentary in quality, of unfixed nature, not single, inert, seen like a pot. How can it be the Self, the knower of changes of things?

The body with hands, feet and the like is not the Self, because life persists even when a limb is missing, and because the powers (of the organs) do not perish; the ruler is not to be ruled (by them).
The Self, the witness of the body, its properties, its actions and its states, has a distinctness from them that is self-evident, being the Real.
A heap of bones, smeared with flesh, full of filth, exceedingly impure — how can this be the knower, who is different from it?
Fools take a heap of skin, flesh, fat, bone and excrement to be "I"; the thoughtful person knows his own nature, the ultimate reality, as different.

I am the body is the idea of the ignorant; for the (half-)learned, "I" is in the body and the soul; for the great soul with discriminating knowledge, the conviction "I am Brahman" is in the true Self.
Give up, O dull-witted, the idea of the Self in this heap of skin, flesh, fat, bone and excrement; fix it in Brahman, the Self of all, free of distinctions, and attain supreme peace.

As long as the wise man does not give up the sense of "I" born of delusion in the unreal body, senses and the rest, so long there is no talk of liberation for him, even if he sees the end of the Vedanta reasoning.
As you have no sense of self in the shadow-body, the body of a reflection, the dream-body, or in a body imagined in the heart, so let it not be in the living body.

The idea of the body as the Self is the seed of the pain of birth and the rest for people of wrong understanding; therefore give it up with effort — when that mind is given up, there is no hope of rebirth.
This breath, joined with the five organs of action, is the sheath made of breath, by which the food-made (sheath), fully pervaded, acts in all its activities.

The Self is not the breath-made either; it is a modification of air, going and coming like the wind, within and without, since it knows nothing anywhere — of what is desired or undesired, of itself or another — being always dependent on another.

The organs of knowledge together with the mind form the mind-made sheath, the cause of the division of things into "mine" and "I," strong, made of distinctions such as names; it swells filling the sheath before it.
Fed by the five organs, the five priests, with the stream of ghee that is objects, blazing with the fuel of many habit-impressions, the mind-made fire burns up the world.

The mind-made fire burns; there is no ignorance other than the mind — the mind itself is ignorance, the cause of bondage; when it is destroyed everything is destroyed, and when it spreads everything spreads.

In dream, where there are no objects, the mind alone creates by its own power the whole world of enjoyer and the rest. In the same way in waking there is no difference; all this is the expansion of the mind.
In deep sleep, when the mind has dissolved, nothing exists, as is universally known. Hence the worldly existence of a person is only imagined by the mind and has no reality.
The cloud is brought by the wind and again carried off by that same wind; bondage is imagined by the mind, and by the same, liberation.
Having imagined attachment to the body and all objects, it binds the person like a beast with a rope; then, having made them distasteful like poison, that same mind releases him from bondage.
Therefore the mind is the cause of a creature's bondage and liberation: stained by the quality of rajas it is the cause of bondage; pure, free of rajas and tamas, of liberation.
Through the excess of discrimination and dispassion, the mind attains purity and becomes fit for liberation; hence the wise seeker of liberation must first make these two firm.
The mind is a great tiger that roams in the forest-lands of objects; let the good who desire liberation not go there.
The mind gives rise to all objects for the enjoyer — gross and subtle — and to the divisions of body, caste, stage of life and birth, and always to qualities, actions, causes and results.

Deluding this attachment-free consciousness, binding it with the qualities of body, senses and breath, the mind makes it wander ceaselessly with "I" and "mine" in its own works and enjoyment of results.

A person's worldly existence is due to the fault of superimposition; the bondage of superimposition is imagined by this (mind) alone. For the undiscriminating one with the faults of rajas and tamas, this is the cause of the pain of birth and the rest.
Therefore the wise, seers of the truth, call the mind ignorance, by which the world is made to whirl like a mass of clouds by the wind.
That mind should be purified with effort by the seeker of liberation; when it is pure, liberation is like a fruit in the palm of the hand.

He who, through sole attachment to liberation, has uprooted desire for objects and renounced all works, and who, with true faith, is devoted to hearing and the rest, shakes off the rajas-nature of the intellect.
The mind-made (sheath) cannot be the Supreme Self either, because it has beginning and end, is subject to change, is of the nature of pain, and is an object; for the seer is never seen as an object.
The intellect with the organs of knowledge and its functions, characterised by agency, is the knowledge-made sheath, the cause of a person's worldly existence.

Following the reflected power of consciousness, the modification of Nature called knowledge, endowed with knowledge and action, constantly and intensely identifies itself as "I" with body, senses and the rest.
This soul, of the nature of "I," from beginningless time, carries on all activity; with past impressions it performs deeds, meritorious and otherwise, and their results.
It enjoys in varied births, going and coming, going out down and up; to this knowledge-made one belong the states of waking, dream and the rest, and the experience of pleasure and pain.

The pride in duties and works belonging to body and stage of life, constantly "mine" — this knowledge-sheath, very luminous through the close proximity of the Supreme Self, becomes its limiting adjunct, so that through delusion the Self's notion of itself falls into transmigration.
This knowledge-made one that shines in the breaths and the heart is a light; being self-luminous and unchanging, the Self, abiding in the adjunct, becomes agent and enjoyer.
Having, by the fault of identification, come to be limited by the intellect, the Self, though the Self of all, falsely sees itself as separate from itself, like pots made of clay.

By connection with the adjunct, the Supreme Self appears to have the adjunct's properties, as fire appears to have the properties of the iron it heats — though by nature ever of one form, supreme, unchanging.
The disciple said: Whether through delusion or otherwise, let the soul's state be that of the Supreme Self; since its adjunct is beginningless, what is beginningless is not held to be destroyed.
Therefore for it the state of individual soul is also eternal, and worldly existence would not cease; then how is there liberation for me? Tell me, revered teacher.
The revered teacher said: You have asked well, wise one; listen with attention: a conception made by one deluded by error is not valid.
Without delusion, no connection with objects could arise for the unattached, actionless, formless Self, as with blueness in space.

The individual-soul state reached by delusion, of the seer, who is his own self — without qualities, without action, whose nature is the inner awareness and bliss of the intellect — is not true; with the removal of delusion it does not exist, since it is of the nature of the unreal.

As long as the delusion, so long is its existence, born of false knowledge and negligence; the snake in the rope lasts only as long as the delusion, and with the destruction of the delusion the snake is no more — so too here.
The beginninglessness of ignorance is admitted, and so of its effect; but when knowledge has arisen, what is due to ignorance, though beginningless, (ends).
On awakening, everything, like a dream, is destroyed together with its root; though beginningless, this is not eternal — clearly, like prior non-existence.
Even of the beginningless, destruction is seen — as of prior non-existence — that which is imagined in the Self through connection with the adjunct of the intellect.
